transcript:
Meeting Header: Date: 2026-06-30 15:00 PDT | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Evan (Cascade Head of ML), Priya (Platform Eng), Daniel (Security)

Summary: Demo focused on schema-bound tool invocation (JSON mode), how Console surfaces contracts and rollouts, and Optimize's recommendations for cost/latency. Customer is interested in a pilot and has security/VPC constraints.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro from our side - I'm Maya Chen, AE at Redwood, and Jordan our SE will drive the demo. Evan, do you want to quick intro?
[00:12] Evan: Yeah sure, Evan Brooks, Head of ML at Cascade. We're building a customer-facing recommendation microservice, need tight 95th percentile latency and deterministic outputs so ops can validate.
[00:22] Priya: Priya here, platform eng, we'll own the VPC/private deployment if we go that route.
[00:26] Daniel: Daniel Ruiz, security lead - focused on encryption in transit & at rest, audit logs, and SAML.
[00:31] Jordan: Awesome. Quick agenda: show JSON mode + schema enforcement for tool calling, demo Console rollouts and live fallback, then Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization. We'll leave time for Qs.

[01:05] Jordan: Alright jumping in - JSON mode is basically a typed output mode where you define a schema for the model output. It helps when your downstream tooling expects strict shapes. So instead of free-form text, you get a validated JSON payload.
[01:23] Evan: How strict is the schema? If model marginally deviates does it fail the whole response?
[01:28] Jordan: Good q. We support strict enforcement, and also tolerant modes. Strict will return a validation error which you can map to a fallback tool call. The typical pattern is schema-first validation plus a structured fallback.

[02:05] Maya: To ground this, Jordan's going to demo a live example: an invoice extractor that needs to call a downstream invoice-normalizer tool and a payments check tool, both exposed as Redwood functions.
[02:20] Jordan: Sharing my screen - console -> API keys -> sample app. Here's the JSON contract: it expects {invoice_id: string, total_cents: integer, vendor: {name: string, tax_id?: string}} and a 'confidence' field.
[02:45] Jordan: Now I run the prompt. Note: we've got the contract registered so the runtime will only allow the model to emit the keys specified, and the tool-caller will only call tools that match the declared action schema.

[03:12] (typing noises)
[03:20] Jordan: Ok results streaming... we got a structured response. Console also shows the validation badge - green = passes.
[03:30] Priya: If it fails validation what happens in production? Do you get logs?
[03:36] Jordan: Yes. You'll get an event entry with the raw model output, the validation errors, and trace id. The Console shows token-level cost, latency, and the validation error; logs are retained per your retention policy.

[04:10] Evan: How does the tool-calling auth work? We need to make sure the model can't call arbitrary endpoints.
[04:16] Jordan: Good point - tools are declared in the model's execution policy. Each tool has an allowlist and role-based permissions. On private deployments we can integrate with your service mesh or use short-lived service tokens.

[04:45] Daniel: On the security front: we need KMS integration, customer-managed keys, and a pull of all requests for audit. Does Redwood support CMK + HSM?
[04:53] Maya: Yes. Private can be configured with KMS/HSM; hosted supports envelope encryption with Redwood KMS but we offer Bring-Your-Own-KMS options for Private. We'll send the security pack.

[05:20] Jordan: Back to the demo - now I'll show a canary rollout. In Console you can create a route that maps 'invoice-extractor' to two model variants. We'll do 5% traffic to new quantized variant with an automatic fallback to the prior model on high error rate.
[05:39] Jordan: Starting rollout... traffic shifting... observability shows per-route latency and per-token cost.
[05:55] Priya: That observability is per-model-per-route? Can we tag by customer id?
[06:00] Jordan: Yes you can add tags and metadata in the request; billing and traces can be filtered by tags, token counts, and route.

[06:30] Evan: A real concern is latency at 95th. Your Optimize product recommends batching but batching might increase P95. How do you balance?
[06:39] Jordan: Exactly the tradeoff. Optimize gives workload-specific batching windows; it recommends small batching for low-latency tail and larger batching for high-throughput endpoints. You can set latency SLOs per route, and the runtime will adapt batching to meet the SLO where possible.

[07:05] Jordan: Also prefix caching and KV cache for prompt prefixes. For chat-like flows we persist the KV cache across requests to avoid recomputing early layers.
[07:16] Evan: When you say KV cache, is that the kv cache on GPU or an external store? We worry about cold starts.
[07:22] Jordan: It's on the serving nodes primarily, with optional warmup from a persisted store. Note sometimes docs say K V cash, haha the transcript auto-snipe. But long story short: we minimize cold-starts via persistent warmup.

[07:45] (laughter)

[08:05] Jordan: Now demoing function/tool calling security: I'm going to purposefully make the model emit an invalid tax_id type to provoke a validation error.
[08:18] (typing)
[08:27] Jordan: There - validation failed. Console shows the error and triggers the fallback: it calls the 'human-review' tool which creates a ticket in your downstream system.
[08:38] Priya: Nice. So fallback is configurable per-contract?
[08:41] Jordan: Yes you can set fallback policies - canary to manual review, auto-normalize, or call a safe function.

[09:05] Evan: For the pilot we want to test both hosted and private. We expect sensitive PII in some fields, so private is a must for those flows. What's the onboarding timeline for private?
[09:16] Maya: Typical private onboarding with VPC peering and KMS takes 4-8 weeks depending on approvals. Dedicated GPU pool options can be faster if you choose reserved capacity. We'll scope that in the SOW.

[09:45] Daniel: Regarding logs - we need full request/response audit trail, immutable. Retention default 90d but can be extended?
[09:53] Jordan: Yes extendable. For enterprise we offer extended retention, and immutability via append-only storage. We'll include audit log options in the security pack.

[10:20] Jordan: Switching gears to runtimes and quantization: Optimize will recommend a quantized candidate based on your prompt length distribution and quality tolerance. You can run A/B tests and the runtime will fall back automatically if quality regresses.
[10:37] Evan: Do you provide quality metrics? BLEU/Rouge aren't always good for our domain.
[10:42] Jordan: Right. We integrate with your eval harness or Redwood's evals, you can upload seed prompts and expected outputs and get regression alerts. We also compute heuristics: schema pass rate, edit distance on structured fields, and domain-specific scoring if you upload a scorer.

[11:15] Priya: On integration, do we need to rework our microservice to call Redwood SDK or can we use generic HTTP?
[11:21] Maya: Both. We have SDKs but the API is REST/HTTP-first so it's easy to integrate with existing services.

[11:40] Evan: For the tool calling interface, how are tools registered? Is that in console or via API?
[11:46] Jordan: Both. In Console you can create tool entries, specify method, args, and RBAC. They get a stable tool-id that your model runtime can call. You can also register via the API for automation.

[12:05] Daniel: One more security: SAML & SCIM for provisioning?
[12:10] Maya: Yes we support SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning. We'll include the integration guide.

[12:30] (Jordan moves to a deeper example)
[12:40] Jordan: Here's a slightly more complex flow: the model must decide between calling 'price-check' tool vs 'manual-quote' tool based on rules encoded in the schema and a small decision tree. The schema enforces the 'decision' enum and the tool arguments.
[12:58] Jordan: I'm going to show how the runtime prevents unauthorized tool calls: the model tried to call an 'admin-delete' tool in a test - the runtime blocked it and logged a policy violation.

[13:20] Evan: Great, that addresses privilege escalation concerns.

[13:35] Priya: What's the expected throughput we can get on a single Dedicated pool?
[13:40] Jordan: Depends on model size and token mix; for a medium sized open model we can push thousands of requests per GPU per hour with batching. We'll provide performance profiles in the model catalog.

[14:02] Jordan: Now a quick look at Optimize suggestions: based on your sample workload I uploaded earlier, it recommends a quantization level 8-bit + dynamic batching window of 40ms for the 'invoice-extractor' route. It also suggests prefix caching for vendor templates where possible.

[14:30] Evan: That 40ms window - what does that look like in p95?
[14:34] Jordan: In our sim it kept p95 under your 200ms target while lowering per-token cost by ~28%. We'll share the simulation spreadsheet.

[15:00] (screen pauses while Jordan pulls reports)
[15:12] Jordan: Ok showing the Console trace - you can click into a request, see token-level breakdown, which kernels run, where batching happened.
[15:25] Priya: Are those kernel traces available on Private?
[15:28] Jordan: On Private you get the same traces; some low-level GPU telemetry may be redacted depending on your compliance posture, but we provide the necessary telemetry for debugging and SLOs.

[15:50] Evan: For pilot acceptance criteria we'll want: 1) p95 < 200ms for the public path, 2) schema pass rate > 98%, 3) audit logs available, 4) security sign-off. Can we commit to that for pilot?
[16:03] Maya: We can commit to running benchmarks against your corpus and aiming for those numbers; final acceptance depends on dataset and pilot infra but we'll treat those as targets.

[16:20] Daniel: The list of audit items I'll need: encryption specs, KMS integration, list of logs and retention, pen-test reports.
[16:28] Maya: We'll attach the security pack and SOC2 artifacts; Daniel please send an initial list and we'll map it.

[17:00] Evan: One operational question - when a schema changes do you support gradual migrations?
[17:06] Jordan: Yes - Console supports schema versioning and you can roll a new schema with a compatibility policy. Runtime can coerce older outputs when backwards compatible or send validation errors otherwise.

[17:30] Priya: If we run on-hosted first and then move to Private, is there migration pain?
[17:35] Jordan: We designed it to be low friction: same API and config. Private adds VPC/KMS/networking steps. Model pinning and routing rules move with the config.

[18:05] (customer asks about rate limits and quotas)
[18:12] Maya: Hosted has rate limits and quotas per account; Dedicated gives predictable throughput without burst throttles. We'll show quota options in the SOW.

[18:40] Evan: Any known gotchas for our use case?
[18:43] Jordan: Watch out for prompt prefix variability - if your invoices vary a lot prefix cache hit-rate drops and cost goes up. Also tool argument types must be strict; a mismatch can cause silent failures if you use tolerant mode.

[19:10] (long pause while Jordan runs another demo flow)
[19:30] Jordan: Quick note - we've seen transcription systems sometimes mis-label product names like Redwood 'Optimize' as 'opt eyes' - sorry that was the transcript earlier.

[19:45] Priya: (laughs) makes sense.

[20:00] Evan: Let's talk commercial - what's the pilot pricing?
[20:05] Maya: For pilots we usually offer a time-bound reserved capacity bundle + usage. I'll send a proposal. Pricing varies whether you go hosted vs dedicated vs private.

[20:28] Evan: For dedicated we'll likely need commit for predictability.

[20:34] Maya: Understood. We'll include commitment tiers and conversion paths in the SOW.

[21:00] (customer asks about rate-limiting token budgets per-route)
[21:06] Jordan: You can set per-route quotas and alerts. Console also supports token-level budgets for teams.

[21:30] (discussion shifts to fallback orchestration)
[21:40] Jordan: One last technical note: fallback orchestration can be chained. Example: schema validation error -> call auto-normalize tool -> if confidence low -> escalate to human review. All steps are auditable.

[22:05] Daniel: For escalation flows, are human-review tickets created in our JIRA?

[22:10] Jordan: Yes - the example uses a 'create-ticket' tool that integrates with Jira or ServiceNow via webhook.

[22:30] Evan: I'd like to see a benchmark plan. Jordan, can you outline steps?

[22:36] Jordan: Sure - 1) ingest your sample prompt set and traffic profile; 2) run hosted baseline on selected model; 3) run quantized/dedicated configs; 4) capture p50/p95, token cost, schema pass rate; 5) deliver spreadsheet and traces. We usually take 48 hours for an initial pass.

[23:05] Priya: We have a larger compliance committee; after the pilot they'll want to see the security deep dive.

[23:12] Maya: We'll schedule that with our security SMEs.

[23:40] (wrap-up)
[23:45] Maya: Recap: Redwood will send SOW + pilot pricing; Jordan will run the bench and share the sim spreadsheet; Daniel will send security checklist; we aim to start bench week of 7/6. Anything to add?

[23:58] Evan: No, that covers it. Thanks, good session.

[24:05] Maya: Thanks all. Closing notes - we'll follow up in email with links to the Console video and security pack.

[24:12] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription had a few recognition errors around acronyms and product names; speaker labels are mostly accurate though sometimes generic.
